setup.zh: 你浮上水面的时候，日头已经落尽了。那口鼎跟着你浮了上来，越浮越小，落在你手心里，沉甸甸的，暖的。
setup.en: By the time you surface, the sun has set. The cauldron rises with you, smaller and smaller, and lands in your palm, heavy and warm.

recap.zh: 第一鼎归来，木牌亮了第二条尾巴；柳树底下站着一个白衣人：「太一宫，赵昂。」「因为天下，该归于一。」他剑鞘头上錾着那个记号：「宫里的印。」
recap.en: The first cauldron came home and a second tail lit on the token; under the willow stood a man in white: "Taiyi Palace. Zhao Ang." "Because all under heaven should be one." He had that mark on his scabbard tip: "The Palace's seal."

zh: 木牌上，第二条尾巴亮了。
en: A cauldron the size of a palm, warm.
On the token, a second tail alight.
Under the willow, someone in white.

story.zh:
小满浮上水面的时候，日头已经落尽了，天边只剩一抹暗红。那口鼎跟着他浮了上来，越浮越小，浮出水面时只有巴掌大，落在他手心里，沉甸甸的，暖的。

胸口的木牌烫得前所未有，他低头一看，木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，第二条亮了。木牌背面秘境里裂开的那道细纹，也合上了；头一条尾巴上暗了这些年的那一截，跟着亮了回来。
story.en:
When Xiaoman surfaced, the sun had set, with only a streak of dark red left at the sky's edge. The cauldron rose with him, growing smaller, and when it broke the surface it was the size of a palm; it landed in his hand, heavy and warm.

The token at his chest burned as never before; he looked down, and of the nine tails of the little curled fox on it, a second was alight. The hairline crack on the back of the token, from the secret realm, had closed; and the stretch of the first tail that had gone dark all these years lit up again.

exits.means: takes up the cauldron, keeps it, faces the stranger in white

story.zh:
那人站在岸边一株老柳树底下，一身白衣，腰悬长剑，正是方才上游柳树底下那一个。

他的目光，落在小满手心里那口巴掌大的鼎上，开口第一句话，却是：「多谢。」

小满一怔：「谢什么？」那人道：「二十五年，宫里请不动他。你一个上午，就把他请上来了。」他往前走了两步，月光照在他腰间那柄剑的剑鞘上，剑鞘头上刻着一个记号：一个圆圈，圈里一横。「太一宫，赵昂。」

太一宫，这三个字小满听过不止一回；从宫里的人自己嘴里报出来，这是头一回。眼前这一个，小满的神识探过去，只探得出是筑基，再往里便是一片雾，探不到底；听那口气，不是跑腿的。

小满攥紧了手里的鼎，道：「你们拿姑娘砸了他二十五年。二十五个姑娘。今天城楼底下，还压死了一个卖豆腐的。」

赵昂的眉头动了一动。那一下极快，快得小满几乎以为是月光晃的。他的眼睛往城西水门那边偏了一偏，又收了回来。他道：「……二十五个。」隔了一会儿，又道：「宫里有位执事，年年入秋到这城里来，住到十月十八。二十五年。我来了半个月，他怎么办差，我没问。」他说完这一句，脸上便又什么都没有了，目光重新落回那口鼎上，道：「这东西，该归太一宫。」

小满道：「为什么？」

赵昂这才正眼看了他，道：「因为天下，该归于一。」

小满怀里的银月，猛地一颤。

「在九天之上。」银月一字一字地道，「那道光劈下来的时候，光里那个声音，说的就是这一句：天下，该归于一。」

赵昂看不见银月，也听不见她说话，他只看见小满抱着一团湿衣裳，脸色一下子变了。他的手，慢慢地按上了剑柄。

小满的眼睛往下一落，落在赵昂按着的那口剑上：剑鞘头上錾着一个圈，圈里一横。赵昂顺着他的眼睛低头看了一眼，脸上第一回有了一点东西，说不清是惊，还是别的什么。他道：「宫里的印。」

小满道：「开山门那天，泗水码头上，一个穿白的拿一锭银子，从一个石匠手里换走了一个五六岁的娃。那锭银子底下，也錾着这个。」他看着赵昂，「那娃叫小豆。是你们的人么？」

赵昂没有答。月光底下，他那张好看的脸，一点一点地白了下去。过了很久，他才道：「……宫里的孩子，没有名字。」

小满没有再问。他听明白了：小豆在宫里，没有名字；说这话的人，大约也是宫里的孩子。

赵昂盯着他，按在剑柄上的手松了又紧，终于放了下来，道：「今日冰夷护着你。我不跟一条河打架。」他转过身去，走了两步，又停住，头也不回地道：「这东西，你拿不稳的。」说罢，一步一步走进了柳树后面的黑地里，脚下没有一点声息。

小满站在河边，把这几年里见过的那个记号，一个一个摆在心里：开山门那天码头上塞进一个石匠手里的那一锭，三老匣子里那一锭，赵昂剑鞘头上那一个。买孩子的，是它；拿镜子满山找白狐狸的，是它；拿姑娘砸了冰夷二十五年的，是它。劈断银月尾巴的那道光里，说的也是它：一。

天下，该归于一。他从前只当这是一句好听的话。

灯笼沉下去，河滩上便只剩一个月亮。小满把鼎揣进怀里，转身要走，脚底下的水，不响了。

浅水里那几根水草，直直地立了起来，像插在冰里。

他认得这个。五年前，泗水渡口。

柳树底下那一条瘦长的影子，又在了。这一回它没退，从柳荫里走出来，一步，一步，走到月亮底下，一身白衣，一张白得看不出年纪的脸，手里托着一面铜镜，镜面朝上，像托着一碗水。他看着小满，嗓子还是那口老井：

「找着了。」

周衡的账簿「啪」地合上了。阿禾蹲在水边，手按在泥里，没有抬头。银月在他衣襟里，一根毛也没动，只低低地道：「这一回，本王不出去。」顿了一顿，「你自己来。」

老井又道：「你筑了基。跑得动了。」他抬起下巴，望了一眼漳水当中，「可方才那一道光，冲上天去，三百里外都看得见。」

他抬起一根指头。

五年前，小满没看见这根指头是怎么到他胸口的。这一回，他看见了——筑了基，眼睛是新的——那根指头还没动，老井身上那一层光，先往指尖上一涌。他的脚已经动了：九宫在心里铺开，他站的是坎一，往巽四上一斜，左脚先出，右脚绕过去。那根指头点空了，点在他身后的柳树上，柳树「咔嚓」一声，齐腰断了，一棵树横着砸进了河里。

老井看着那棵树，道：「嗯，长本事了。」

他把那面铜镜翻了过来。一道冷光打出来，不打人，直奔小满的胸口，奔木牌去。小满的右手早在怀里了，摸出来的是那面自拍镜碎下来的一瓣——七八瓣里最大的一瓣，他揣了五年——迎了上去。

这面破铜碎成了一瓣，也只会一样：什么光打上来，原样扔回去。

「嗡」的一声，那道光折了回去，一头撞回老井手里那面镜子上。镜子当中「咔」地一响，裂开一道缝，从镜心直裂到镜沿。老井低头看了一眼那道缝，脸上头一回有了一样东西：不是怒，是心疼，像一个穷人看着一只摔了的碗。

就这一眼的工夫，小满拔出了火柴。可老井抬起头来的时候，那只手已经到了：不是指头，是一整只手掌，平平地推过来，嘴唇动了一动，小满没听清他念的是什么。他拿剑去挡——剑挡住了，人没挡住。那一掌推在剑上，剑推在他胸口上，他整个人飞了出去，听见自己左边肩膀「咯」了一声，落进了漳水里。

水把他接住了。不冷，凉的，托着他，像一只手。他在水里翻过身来，嘴里一股血腥气。岸上，老井走到了水边，站住了，没有下水。他低头看着脚尖前头那一线水，看了一会儿，没有往前迈。

他抬起那只手，冲着水里的小满，要再推一掌。

便在这时，岸边那一排老柳树底下，泥里「噗噗」地拱起一片树根，又粗又黑，一根缠住他的脚脖子，一根勒上他抬起来的那条胳膊，把那一掌，往旁边一扯——就扯了那么一霎。阿禾还蹲在原地，手按在泥里，红鼻头冻得通红，眼睛望着别处，像一个吓傻了的练气小丫头。

那一霎，老井一身的灵力，全涌在那条抬起来的胳膊上，跟树根较劲；肩膀上那一层光，跟着薄了一薄。

石头的缝，树的缝，熊身上的缝。小满从水里站了起来。他没砍，是送——火柴顺着那薄了一霎的地方进去，像风钻进了门缝，从肩膀上进去，从腋下出来。

那条胳膊，连着缠在上头的树根，一齐掉进了漳水里。水面上冒了一个泡，便什么也没有了。

老井没有叫。他看着自己那半截袖子，袖口空空的，往下滴着血。他又抬头看了看河心——河心那片黑水底下，两盏青灯笼，一盏一盏，又亮了起来。

他往后退了一步，退进了柳荫里。那口老井嗓子从黑地里传出来，还是平平的，一个字也没散：

「这一笔，记下了。」

柳荫里，没有人了。

小满站在齐腰深的水里，火柴还举着，举了很久，才放下来。左边那条胳膊吊在身子旁边，抬不起来；一张嘴，又吐了一口血。阿禾蹚进水里来，一把架住了他，手按在他肩膀上，按得很重，嘴里念的还是那一句：观天之道。她的手在抖。

「……谁教你往水里跳的？」

小满道：「……娘。打不过就跑。」

阿禾没说话，把他往岸上拖。周衡站在岸上，抱着账簿，一张脸白得跟那人差不多。他翻开账簿，手抖着，提起笔来，半天，没落下去。

小满坐在岸边，看着那一线水。五年前，泗水渡口，那一根指头，他连看也没看见；今天，他看见了，躲开了，还还了一剑。还是打不过，还是跑了，还是叫人拖上来的。可下一回——

下一回，他得是站着的。
story.en:
The man stood under an old willow at the water's edge, all in white, a long sword at his waist — the same one who had stood under the willows upstream.

His eyes fell on the palm-sized cauldron in Xiaoman's hand, and the first thing he said was: "Thank you."

Xiaoman was startled: "For what?" The man said: "For twenty-five years the Palace couldn't get him to come up. You did it in one morning." He took two steps forward; moonlight fell on the scabbard at his waist, and on its tip was a mark: a circle, with one bar inside it. "Taiyi Palace. Zhao Ang."

Taiyi Palace — Xiaoman had heard the name more than once; this was the first time one of its own people had said it aloud. Xiaoman reached for this one with his spirit sense: Foundation, that much he could read; past it lay only fog, no bottom to be found. By his tone, he was no errand boy.

Xiaoman gripped the cauldron in his hand: "You battered him with girls for twenty-five years. Twenty-five girls. And today a tofu-seller was crushed under the tower."

Zhao Ang's brows moved — so quickly Xiaoman almost thought it was the moonlight shifting. His eyes slid toward the water gate on the west side and came back. He said: "…Twenty-five." After a while: "A steward of the Palace comes to this city every autumn and stays to the eighteenth of the tenth month. Twenty-five years. I have been here half a month; how he does his work, I didn't ask." With that his face was empty again; his eyes went back to the cauldron: "This belongs to the Taiyi Palace."

Xiaoman said: "Why?"

Only then did Zhao Ang really look at him: "Because all under heaven should be one."

Yinyue, in Xiaoman's arms, gave a violent start.

"High in the ninth heaven," Yinyue said, word by word. "When that light struck down, the voice in the light said exactly this: all under heaven should be one."

Zhao Ang could not see Yinyue nor hear her speak; he saw only Xiaoman clutching a bundle of wet clothes, his face suddenly changed. His hand slowly came to rest on his sword hilt.

Xiaoman's eyes dropped to the sword under Zhao Ang's hand: on the tip of its scabbard was chiselled a circle, with a bar across it. Zhao Ang followed his look down, and for the first time something showed in his face — surprise, or something else. He said: "The Palace's seal."

Xiaoman said: "The day the gate opened, on the Si River shore, a man in white traded one ingot of silver to a stonemason for a boy of five or six. That ingot had this on its base too." He looked at Zhao Ang. "The boy was called Little Dou. Is he one of yours?"

Zhao Ang did not answer. In the moonlight his handsome face slowly went white. After a long while he said: "…The Palace's children have no names."

Xiaoman asked no more. He understood: in the Palace, Little Dou had no name; and the one saying so was, most likely, a Palace child himself.

Zhao Ang stared at him, his hand on the hilt tightening and loosening, and at last he let it go: "Today Bingyi guards you. I don't fight a river." He turned away, took two steps, stopped, and said without looking back: "You won't be able to hold on to that." Then, step by step, he walked into the dark behind the willows, without a sound underfoot.

Xiaoman stood by the river and laid out in his mind, one by one, every time he had seen that mark these past years: the ingot pressed into a stonemason's hand on the river shore the day the gate opened; the ingot in the Three Elders' casket; the one on the tip of Zhao Ang's scabbard. What bought children was it; what combed the mountains with a mirror for a white fox was it; what battered Bingyi with girls for twenty-five years was it. And in the light that cut off Yinyue's tails, what the voice said was it too: one.

All under heaven should be one. He had once taken it for a fine-sounding phrase.

When the lanterns had sunk, only the moon was left on the shore. Xiaoman tucked the cauldron into his jacket and turned to go, and the water under his feet went quiet.

The few strands of weed in the shallows stood straight up, as if set in ice.

He knew this. Five years ago, the Si ferry.

That long thin shadow under the willows was there again. This time it didn't draw back. It came out of the willow shade, one step, one step, into the moonlight: a white robe, a face so white it had no age, a bronze mirror held face-up in one hand as if he carried a bowl of water. He looked at Xiaoman, and the voice was still that old well:

"You found it."

Zhou Heng's ledger shut with a slap. A-He crouched at the water's edge, hand pressed into the mud, and didn't look up. Inside his jacket Yinyue didn't stir a hair; she only said, low: "This time I'm not coming out." A pause. "Do it yourself."

The old well said, "You've built your foundation. You can run now." He lifted his chin toward the middle of the Zhang. "But that light just now went up to the sky. It could be seen three hundred li off."

He raised one finger.

Five years ago Xiaoman hadn't seen how that finger reached his chest. This time he saw it — foundation built, the eyes were new — before the finger moved, the layer of light on the man surged toward its tip. His feet were already moving: the nine palaces spread out in his mind; he stood on Kan One, and slanted onto Xun Four, left foot first, the right circling round. The finger struck empty air, struck the willow behind him, and the willow snapped at the waist with a crack and went down across the river.

The old well looked at the tree. "Mm. You've grown."

He turned the bronze mirror over. A cold light shot out — not at the man, straight at Xiaoman's chest, at the token. Xiaoman's right hand was already inside his jacket; what came out was a shard of the selfie mirror — the biggest of the seven or eight, carried five years — and he met the light with it.

Broken down to one shard, this bronze still knew only one trick: whatever light struck it, it threw straight back.

With a hum the light folded back and slammed into the mirror in the old well's hand. There was a crack in the middle of it, and a split ran from the centre to the rim. The old well looked down at the split, and for the first time something showed on his face: not anger — heartache, like a poor man looking at a dropped bowl.

In that one look Xiaoman drew Matchstick. But when the old well raised his head, the hand had already come: not a finger, a whole palm, pushed flat toward him, the lips moving once — Xiaoman didn't catch what he said. He blocked with the sword — the sword held; the boy didn't. The palm drove the sword, the sword drove into his chest, he flew backward, heard his left shoulder go with a crack, and came down in the Zhang.

The water caught him. Not cold — cool, holding him up like a hand. He rolled over in it, blood in his mouth. On the bank the old well walked to the water's edge and stopped, and didn't step in. He looked down at the line of water in front of his toes, looked a while, and didn't step.

He raised that hand toward Xiaoman in the water, for a second palm.

At that moment, under the row of old willows on the bank, roots came heaving out of the mud — thick and black — one wrapping his ankle, one cinching the arm he had raised, dragging that palm aside: for just an instant. A-He was still crouched where she had been, hand in the mud, nose red with cold, eyes turned elsewhere, like a scared little girl at some low layer of qi.

In that instant all the old well's power flooded into the raised arm, straining against the roots; the light on his shoulder thinned with it.

The seam in the stone, the seam in the tree, the seam in the bear. Xiaoman stood up out of the water. He didn't cut — he sent: Matchstick went in through the place that had thinned for an instant, like wind slipping through a door-crack, in at the shoulder and out under the arm.

The arm, with the roots still wound round it, fell into the Zhang. A bubble came up on the water, and then there was nothing.

The old well didn't cry out. He looked at his half sleeve, the cuff hanging empty, dripping blood. Then he looked up at the middle of the river — under that dark water, two green lanterns, one and then the other, were lighting up again.

He stepped back, into the willow shade. The old-well voice came out of the dark, still flat, not one word frayed:

"This one I'll write down."

In the willow shade there was no one.

Xiaoman stood waist-deep in the water with Matchstick still raised, and held it raised a long time before he lowered it. His left arm hung at his side and wouldn't lift; when he opened his mouth he spat blood again. A-He waded in and hooked him under the arm, her hand pressed hard on his shoulder, saying under her breath the same line as ever: Observe the Way of Heaven. Her hand was shaking.

"…Who taught you to jump in the river?"

"…Mother," said Xiaoman. "If you can't win, run."

A-He said nothing and dragged him toward the bank. Zhou Heng stood on the shore clutching the ledger, his face as white as the man's. He opened the ledger, hands shaking, raised the brush, and for a long while didn't set it down.

Xiaoman sat at the water's edge and looked at that line of water. Five years ago, at the Si ferry, he hadn't even seen the finger; today he had seen it, dodged it, and given back one cut. He still couldn't win, he had still run, he had still been dragged out. But next time —

Next time, he would have to be standing.

exits.means: hesitates, asks what will happen, wants to wait

text.zh: 它在你掌心里，一明，一暗，像在很慢地呼吸。
text.en: It lies in your palm, light and dark, as if breathing very slowly.
